To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pesticide-degrading potential of microbial communities is affected by competition for macroelements.
The pesticide degradation capacity of microbial communities can be affected by competition with other microorganisms.

(1) competition effects cause the loss of pesticide-degrading capacity in microbial communities, (2) the loss of pesticide degradation can be prevented by the addition of a selective substrate, and (3) the loss of degradation can be detected by the PCR detection of the pesticide-degrading genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of competition with bacteria from ditchwater on a pesticide-hydrolyzing strain.
the effect of the competition for macroelements (C, N and P) with bacteria from ditchwater on a pesticide-degrading strain of the Flavobacteriaceae.

the development of a new approach to improve the pesticide-degrading capacities of microbial communities in the environment by the application of a selective carbon, energy and nitrogen source for the pesticide degraders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the competition effects caused by the bacteria from ditch water can be overcome by addition of selective carbon, nitrogen and phosphorous sources to the chemostat cultures.
the competition for macroelements (nitrogen and phosphate) is the most important factor in determining the survival of the pesticide-degrading strain FB.
the pesticide-degrading capacities of microbial communities are dependent on the frequency of exposure to pesticides.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pesticide degradation capacity of mixed cultures is not stable over a long period of time, but depends on the frequency of the exposure to the pesticide compound.
a high frequency of exposure to a pesticide compound is required to ensure that pesticide-degrading bacteria are retained in a microbial community.
the pesticide degrading capacity of microbial consortia is a function of the frequency of exposure to pesticide compounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
competition for macroelements is an important factor in the survival of pesticide-degrading microorganisms in natural environments.
the presence of a selective substrate can be used to maintain pesticide-degrading microorganisms in mixed cultures.
the presence of the parthion hydrolases gene does not necessarily mean the presence of the corresponding enzyme in the environment.
